top_choice_rationale: P001 (Melitz and Helpman, firm heterogeneity and selection in trade) has a clear, testable central claim: selection into exporting and reallocation across firms raise aggregate productivity and shape the gains from trade. More than twenty years of firm-level data from many countries have repeatedly tested this claim, and the qualitative result has held up even though welfare magnitudes depend on functional form. I count that kind of durability under repeated testing as the strongest evidence of merit. Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI makes him a defensible second name. The framework is also distinct from the 2008 prize, which covered representative-firm new trade theory. The main costs are the uncredited Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum strands and the sensitivity of welfare estimates to assumptions. The citation should be worded around the theoretical framework. P002 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) comes second for its breadth of influence and maturity. Its credit is diffuse across eight names, and micro evidence on state-dependent pricing qualifies Calvo's mechanism. P003 (Kiyotaki and Moore) comes third. It has clean two-author credit and a distinct mechanism, but collateral channels are less cleanly identified than the theory. No award is last because each of the three proposals is a mature and substantive achievement. I have not independently verified citation or priority details. I do not treat the support counts in the slate as merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile for the credited names in P001, P002 or P003 (Melitz, Helpman, Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki, Moore). My listed frequent co-authors (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Johannesson, Rand) are not credited candidates. I disclose SSE ties to Ellingsen and Johannesson, both former committee members, and my metascience orientation, which makes me weight repeated empirical testing heavily. These are not adjudicated.
